Explore the relay server in C:\Users\Ayden's mini\Desktop\GameDev\RockSkipping\relay (server.js plus package.json and any other files). Search breadth: very thorough — read files fully. Also check the repo root README.md and PLAN.md at C:\Users\Ayden's mini\Desktop\GameDev\RockSkipping for architecture notes about the relay and tunneling (cloudflared).

This relay bridges phone controllers (WebSocket) to a Unity game. The user reports significant lag between phone movement and the in-game visual.

Report in detail:
1. The full message flow: how controller messages are received, parsed, and forwarded to the game client; any queuing, batching, setInterval-based forwarding, rate limiting, or throttling.
2. WebSocket library used and options (perMessageDeflate, etc.), HTTP server setup, static file serving.
3. Room/player management: how players join, IDs, what happens on reconnect.
4. Any per-message JSON parse/stringify overhead, logging on hot paths, or O(n) scans per message.
5. Any bugs: memory leaks, dead connections not cleaned up, missed error handling, race conditions.
Include exact line numbers and code snippets for the message forwarding hot path and any constants (intervals, buffer sizes).

content.content:
1	# Rock Skipping
2	
3	A couch party game: the game runs on a PC driving a TV, and players use their phones as
4	motion controllers through a web page — no app download, Jackbox-style.
5	
6	**Read [PLAN.md](PLAN.md) first.** It has the full architecture, the cross-platform sensor
7	problem, the physics design, and the milestone breakdown. This file only covers how to run
8	what currently exists.
9	
10	## Layout
11	
12	| Path | What it is |
13	|---|---|
14	| `Assets/` | Unity 6 project (6000.3.10f1) — the game screen |
15	| `relay/` | Node WebSocket relay, and the HTTP server for the controller page |
16	| `controller/` | Phone controller web app — sensors, throw gestures, join screen |
17	| `PLAN.md` | Full design and implementation plan |
18	
19	## Status
20	
21	**M0 and M1 complete, M2 in progress.** The relay is hardened and tested, the controller
22	app normalizes sensors and sends `AIM`/`THROW`, and the pure skip solver plus the aim
23	preview are in. Verified end to end with one Android phone.
24	
25	Hosting is one click: pressing Play brings up the relay and a public HTTPS tunnel, then
26	puts the room code, join URL and a QR on screen. A match runs a fixed number of rounds and
27	ends with a standings screen — see Match flow below.
28	
29	Still open in M2: `RockDefinition`/`RockSpawner` and the four specials, `RingGate`
30	(nothing publishes `RingPassedEvent` yet, so `ScoreManager.pointsPerRing` is currently
31	dead), and an authored lake scene to replace the runtime placeholder geometry.
32	
33	Not yet run with more than one real player — turn rotation, the spectator view and the
34	results screen are written and unit-tested but have not been exercised at a party.
35	
36	## Running the game
37	
38	Open the **Bootstrap** scene and press Play. `LocalServices` then:
39	
40	1. reuses a relay already listening on `:3000`, or runs `npm install` (first launch only)
41	   and starts one
42	2. starts `cloudflared` and waits for its public `https://….trycloudflare.com` address
43	3. hands the URL to `JoinScreen`, which shows it with the room code and a scannable QR
44	
45	Players scan the QR — it pre-fills the room code via `?room=CODE` — and type only a name.
46	
47	## How aiming works
48	
49	Two conventions have to agree, and both were wrong in the first playtest.
50	
51	**On the phone**, aim is the compass bearing of the direction the top of the phone
52	points — derived from the device's full rotation and projected onto the ground, *not*
53	from the DeviceOrientation `alpha` angle. Alpha is a Euler yaw and is degenerate near
54	vertical: at `beta = 89` a phone reads a bearing of -30°, and at `beta = 91` the same
55	phone reads +150°. A throwing swing sweeps straight through that singularity, so
56	physically straight throws veered hard left or right depending on where in the arc the
57	release landed. `pointingHeading` returns a `confidence` alongside the bearing, and the
58	heading is only updated while the phone is actually pointing at the horizon — through
59	the steep middle of a swing the last good bearing is held. That is what makes "point at
60	the screen and let go" behave.
61	
62	A side effect worth keeping: wrist roll (`gamma`) cannot change where the top of the
63	phone points, so aim is immune to it for free.
64	
65	**In Unity**, `aimDeg = 0` means "along `AimPreview.ThrowForward`", which is derived
66	from the aiming camera flattened onto the horizontal plane. Straight has to mean
67	straight *to the player looking at the TV*; a camera framed even slightly off-axis makes
68	a centred throw visibly drift, and no amount of correct phone aiming can fix it. The
69	preview arc, the ghost rock and the live throw all read the same value, so the preview
70	cannot promise a line the throw does not take.
71	
72	The aiming camera is therefore square on to the lake — identity rotation, looking
73	straight down +Z, so `ThrowForward` comes out as exactly +Z. Keep it that way when the
74	real lake is authored: any yaw left in the aiming view is yaw the player has to
75	unconsciously correct for.
76	
77	The camera only moves while a rock is in flight. Once it has returned it snaps exactly
78	onto the home pose and stops being touched at all — the smoothing used to run every
79	idle frame, and since both interpolations approach their target asymptotically, the
80	aiming view never quite settled.
81	
82	Bearings and Unity's yaw are both clockwise-from-above, so the sign passes straight
83	through. If a platform turns out to disagree, open the controller with `?yawSign=-1` to
84	confirm it on the device before changing any code.
85	
86	## The throw gesture
87	
88	**Point at the lake, hold, swing, let go.** The hold is load-bearing: it is the only
89	window in which the player sees the predicted arc and can adjust before committing.
90	
91	Tap-swing-tap was tried in playtest and reverted. It did not sharpen the release so much
92	as delete the aiming phase — with no hold there is barely any time when the arc is on
93	screen and steady. `?gesture=tap` still opts back into it; `ThrowController` keeps both,
94	along with the two guards tap mode needs (`minArmMs`, so one bouncy tap cannot arm and
95	fire in the same motion; `maxArmMs`, because an armed-and-forgotten throw is invisible
96	when no finger is on the glass and would stall the match).
97	
98	### Aim is live to the last frame, and the throw is that frame
99	
100	Aim tracks the phone continuously, right through the swing, and the throw is computed
101	from the **last sensor sample before release**. Nothing freezes or averages it: the
102	value the player released on is the value that gets thrown.
103	
104	### Heading is integrated from the gyro, not sampled from fused orientation
105	
106	`deviceorientation` is a *fused* estimate: it lags real motion by tens of milliseconds
107	and arrives on its own schedule, independent of `devicemotion`. Reading the heading out
108	of it means every sample carries an angle from a moment ago — during a fast swing, the
109	heading barely moves at all between orientation events, and the release frame reports
110	where the phone was pointing before the swing finished. Fast swings simply got lost.
111	
112	`rotationRate` arrives with `devicemotion` at the full sensor rate and is essentially
113	instantaneous. `headingRateFromGyro` converts it into the rate of change of the pointing
114	bearing, and `MotionSource` integrates that every sample, so the heading is current at
115	the moment of release rather than a stale snapshot.
116	
117	The fused reading is still used, as the drift-free reference — but it corrects the
118	integrated value *in proportion to how slowly the phone is turning*
119	(`FAST_ROTATION_DEG_PER_SEC`). Above that rate it is ignored outright, because snapping
120	to it mid-swing would hand back exactly the lag this exists to remove. Once the phone
121	settles, it reasserts itself and drift goes away.
122	
123	The conversion is the Z-X'-Y'' Euler kinematics:
124	
125	```
126	headingRate = (rotationRate.beta * sin(gamma) - rotationRate.alpha * cos(gamma)) / cos(beta)
127	```
128	
129	Checked numerically against a finite difference of the rotation matrix — exact to
130	~5e-7 deg/s across 600 poses at up to 500 deg/s. The obvious-looking shortcut of taking
131	the world-vertical component of the angular velocity is **wrong**: rolling a tilted phone
132	about its own long axis sweeps a large vertical rotation while the top of the phone does
133	not change heading at all, and that shortcut reports a couple of hundred deg/s of aim
134	drift the player never performed. There is a test for exactly that case.
135	
136	`1/cos(beta)` is the same singularity `pointingHeading` has, so integration is gated on
137	the same forward-lean check.
138	
139	### Aim covers the full rotation
140	
141	`maxAimDeg` is 180, not 45. A 45 degree ceiling silently discarded the top of every fast
142	swing: any turn past it flattened to exactly 45, so hard throws all reported the same aim
143	regardless of where the phone actually pointed. `dYaw` is already a shortest-angle delta
144	in (-180, 180], so nothing is clipped — and aiming behind you is simply allowed.
145	
146	Two more things are sized for aim-stream accuracy:
147	
148	- **AIM streams at 60Hz**, matching the sensor rate, not the 20Hz the plan originally
149	  specified. At 20Hz every frame is up to 50ms stale before it leaves the phone, which
150	  during a swing is degrees of error baked in before the network is involved.
151	- **The relay's rate limit is 180 msg/sec**, not 60. At exactly 60 the limiter began
152	  discarding aim frames as soon as a throw or heartbeat shared the same second — and it
153	  drops silently, so the arc would stutter for reasons that look nothing like rate
154	  limiting from the game side.
155	
156	`AimPreview.smoothTime` is the remaining lag: `SmoothDamp` trails its target by roughly
157	that long, so it wants to be only just large enough to hide packet jitter. It is 0.035s
158	against a 60Hz stream.
159	
160	**On release the arc snaps to the throw that actually happened** and holds there while it
161	fades, redrawn with the throw's real power, timing and spin instead of the nominal ones.
162	So the last thing on screen is the line the rock is genuinely on — which also makes any
163	remaining preview/throw disagreement visible rather than something to squint at frame by
164	frame.
165	
166	While still predicting, power and timing are unknown, so the arc is drawn at a nominal
167	0.7 power with perfect timing. Until release the arc promises a *line*, not a landing
168	spot.
169	
170	## Match flow
171	
172	`TurnManager` owns a three-phase lifecycle, and nothing advances on its own:
173	
174	| Phase | What is on screen | How it advances |
175	|---|---|---|
176	| **Lobby** | room code, join URL, QR, roster | press **Space** to start |
177	| **Playing** | the lake; join details shrink to a corner card | each throw completing rotates the turn |
178	| **Results** | final standings, winner highlighted | press **Space** to play again |
179	
180	A match is `Rounds Per Match` rounds (default 3), each giving every player one throw. The
181	turn advances on `ThrowCompletedEvent` — a sunk rock is what drives the match forward — so
182	**Space** and **N** (force next turn) are the only keys needed to run a session.
183	
184	The match never starts by itself: somebody arriving mid-lobby should not begin it for
185	everyone already waiting. Throws are refused outside the Playing phase, so a stale phone
186	cannot fling rocks across the results screen.
187	
188	### Verifying with a second PC
189	
190	A desktop browser has no motion sensors, so a real swing produces nothing. Rather than
191	letting that seat deadlock the match, `release()` synthesizes a throw from how long the
192	grip button was held — but **only on a device that has never produced a single motion
193	event**, which a phone does within a frame of joining. A weak gesture on a real phone
194	stays a fumble. Simulated throws are labelled on the controller and report zero samples,
195	which is how the TV debug readout (**F1**) tells them apart.
196	
197	So: open the join URL on a second PC, join with a different name, and press Space on the
198	host. Both seats take turns, scores accumulate, and the match ends on the final round.
199	
200	**Requires** Node 20+ and cloudflared:
201	
202	```bash
203	winget install Cloudflare.cloudflared
204	```
205	
206	A tunnel is not optional: phone motion sensors need a secure context, and an HTTPS page
207	cannot open a plain `ws://` socket to a LAN address. Both problems disappear when the page
208	and the socket share one public origin, which is why the relay serves the controller itself.
209	
210	The quick tunnel's hostname is random per launch. Nobody types it — that is what the QR is
211	for — but it does mean a URL from a previous session is dead. For a stable address, switch
212	to a named tunnel; only the `cloudflared` arguments in `LocalServices` change.
213	
214	To run the pieces by hand instead, untick **Start Local Services** on `Bootstrap`.

217	
218	```bash
219	cd relay && npm install && npm start
220	```
221

223	and `/qr`. Deploy with `fly deploy` (see `relay/fly.toml`).
224	
225	Integration tests — routing, identity stamping, reconnect, the QR endpoint, and each
226	hardening fix:
227	
228	```bash
229	cd relay && npm test
230	```
231	
232	## Verifying the Unity event system
233	
234	The event system was ported from FactoryTM and needed four changes to work across scene
235	loads. The verification proves those hold at runtime rather than by inspection.
236	
237	In the editor: **RockSkipping → Verify → Run Event System Verification**. Results land in the
238	Console and in `verification-result.txt`.
239	
240	Headless — note the deliberate absence of `-quit`, since the method enters play mode:
241	
242	```bash
243	"C:\Users\Ayden's mini\Desktop\UnityVersions\6000.3.10f1\Editor\Unity.exe" -batchmode -nographics -projectPath . -executeMethod RockSkippingEditor.ProjectSetup.RunVerification -logFile verify.log
244	```
245	
246	Poll for `verification-result.txt`, then kill the process — exiting the editor from the
247	domain reload that follows play mode is unreliable in batchmode.
248	
249	Expected output:
250	
251	```
252	PASS
253	  PASS  publish/subscribe delivers
254	  PASS  scene-local subscriber receives
255	  PASS  EventManager survived Bootstrap -> Lobby
256	  PASS  persistent subscriber still receives after Lobby load
257	  PASS  EventManager survived Lobby -> Game
258	  PASS  persistent subscriber still receives after Game load
259	  PASS  destroyed subscriber pruned (3 -> 2)
260	  PASS  no publish errors logged
261	```
262	
263	`Assets/Scripts/Verification/` is a scaffolding aid, not shipping code. Delete it once the
264	event system stops changing.
265	
266	## Scenes
267	
268	Build order is **Bootstrap → Lobby → Game → Results**. `Bootstrap` must stay at index 0: it
269	creates the managers that have to outlive scene transitions, then loads `Lobby`.
270	
271	`RelayClient` is created in `Bootstrap` alongside the other persistent managers. It must
272	stay there: if it lives in a scene instead, the WebSocket is torn down on every transition
273	and every phone bounces back to the join screen — which looks like a networking bug but is
274	a lifecycle one. The same applies to `LocalServices`, which owns the two child processes,
275	and `JoinScreen`, so a latecomer can still scan in during the Game scene.
276	
277	## Notes for whoever picks this up
278	
279	- The project is on the **built-in render pipeline**, not URP as PLAN.md assumes. Switching
280	  is cheapest right now while there are no materials to break.
281	- Every scene-local subscriber must call `EventManager.Instance?.UnsubscribeFromAllEvents(this)`
282	  in `OnDestroy`. The destroyed-subscriber fix backstops forgetting, but don't rely on it.
283	- `EventManager.DebugLoggingEnabled` is exposed on the `Bootstrap` component. Turn it on
284	  while wiring new events — publish failures are otherwise swallowed into `Debug.LogError`.

30	
31	## Architecture
32	
33	Three separately-deployed components:
34	
35	```
36	  Phone (Safari/Chrome)          Relay (Node+ws)           Unity 6 Desktop
37	  Cloudflare Pages, HTTPS   <--wss-->   Fly.io    <--wss-->   TV / PC
38	  normalizes sensors                 routes by room         simulates physics
39	```
40	
41	**Connection flow:**
42	1. Unity boots → connects to relay → `CREATE_ROOM` → relay generates and returns a 4-letter code
43	2. TV displays the code, the controller URL, and a QR code
44	3. Phone opens URL → enters code (QR pre-fills it) → `JOIN_ROOM`
45	4. Relay notifies Unity `PLAYER_JOINED`
46	5. Phone streams aim + sends throws → relay → Unity
47	6. Unity broadcasts turn/score/spectator state → relay → phones
48	
49	**Authority model: the PC is authoritative for everything.** Phones are dumb input devices; they never simulate. There is no Unity-to-Unity networking anywhere in this project — which has a useful consequence noted under Rock Data below.
50	
51	### Why a hosted relay rather than direct LAN connection
52	
53	Two hard blockers make LAN-direct a dead end:
54	
55	- **iOS requires a secure context for motion sensors.** You cannot obtain a public TLS certificate for `192.168.x.x`. Self-signed means installing a trust profile on every guest's phone, which defeats the "scan and play" premise.
56	- **Mixed content.** Once the controller page is HTTPS (which it must be, per above), the browser blocks it from opening an insecure `ws://` connection to a LAN IP.
57	
58	A public `wss://` relay solves both, and additionally solves NAT traversal so players aren't required to be on the same Wi-Fi.
59	
60	### Why not AirConsole
61	
62	Worth recording since it was the initial instinct. AirConsole is a legitimate option, but games built with its plugin **only run as Unity WebGL builds hosted on AirConsole's own servers**. The cost isn't money — it's WebGL performance limits, slow build iteration, and no path to a Steam release later.
63	
64	Critically, **AirConsole would not have reduced the hard part of this project.** The controller is still your own HTML/JS either way; AirConsole solves HTTPS, pairing, and transport, which Cloudflare Pages plus a small relay also solve. The cross-platform sensor normalization work below is identical under both.
65	
66	---
67	
68	## The motion pipeline
69	
70	This is the hard part of the project and the main technical risk. Budget accordingly.
71	
72	### The cross-platform problem
73	
74	iOS and Android disagree in ways that will silently produce wrong behaviour rather than errors:
75	
76	| Behavior | iOS | Android |
77	|---|---|---|
78	| `DeviceMotionEvent.acceleration` | **Not available** | Available |
79	| `accelerationIncludingGravity` | Available | Available |
80	| `requestPermission()` | Required, must follow a user touch | **API does not exist** |
81	| Compass heading | `webkitCompassHeading`, true north, **clockwise** | `alpha`, magnetic north, **counter-clockwise** |
82	| Vibration | Unreliable | Works |
83	
84	Two of these are landmines:
85	
86	- **iOS has no `acceleration` property**, only the gravity-inclusive one. Code developed on Android will read `undefined` on every iPhone. Use `accelerationIncludingGravity` on both platforms and remove gravity manually.
87	- **Compass heading runs in opposite directions** on the two platforms, off different norths. Any aiming logic built on absolute yaw will steer backwards on one platform.
88	
89	Also note `requestPermission()` **throws** on Android if called unconditionally — it must be feature-detected.
90	
91	### Test device policy — Android only for now
92	
93	**No iOS device is available to test on.** That constrains what any milestone can honestly claim:
94	
95	- **All testing and every acceptance criterion is Android (Chrome).** A milestone is "done" when it works on Android. Do not gate progress on iOS behaviour that cannot be observed.
96	- **iOS code paths are still written, but treated as unverified.** The permission gate, the `accelerationIncludingGravity` fallback, and the compass-heading handling all go in now — writing them later means retrofitting the normalization layer, which is exactly the rework this design exists to avoid. They are implemented from spec and marked as untested.
97	- **Every iOS-specific branch carries an `// UNVERIFIED (iOS):` comment** naming what it assumes. That makes the untested surface greppable the day a device shows up, instead of a hunt through the whole file.
98	- **Do not claim cross-platform parity.** The 10% iPhone-vs-Android agreement check in Verification is deferred, not passed. Until it runs, treat iOS as designed-for but unproven.
99	
100	The single highest-risk unverified assumption is that **iOS lacks `DeviceMotionEvent.acceleration`**, so the code must never read it. Because Android *does* expose it, an Android-only test will never catch a regression that reintroduces it. Guard this in code rather than by discipline — read `accelerationIncludingGravity` behind one accessor in `sensors.js` and never touch `event.acceleration` anywhere else.
101	
102	When an iPhone becomes available, the catch-up work is: run the same gesture on both devices, compare descriptor values, and confirm the permission prompt appears and is honoured. That is a session's work, not a redesign — provided the branches were written now.
103	
104	### The governing rule
105	
106	**Never send raw sensor values to Unity. Normalize on the phone.**
107	
108	The controller emits device-agnostic values. Unity never sees a platform difference. This is both the correctness fix and a clean reusable abstraction boundary.
109

200	not change bearing at all, and that shortcut invents hundreds of deg/s of aim drift.
201	
202	Lock the page to portrait (`screen.orientation.lock('portrait')` where supported) so `beta`/`gamma` don't swap physical axes mid-throw. Treat the lock as best-effort and keep the rotation compensation in step 3 as the real fix.
203	
204	Permission gate, which must sit behind a real tap:
205	
206	```js
207	async function requestMotion() {
208	  if (typeof DeviceMotionEvent?.requestPermission === 'function') {
209	    const res = await DeviceMotionEvent.requestPermission();   // iOS only
210	    return res === 'granted';
211	  }
212	  return true;   // Android: no permission API
213	}
214	```
215	
216	---
217	
218	## Two-channel input design
219	
220	The aim preview is a **required** feature, so input splits into two channels with deliberately different reliability characteristics.
221	
222	### `AIM` — continuous, lossy, cosmetic only
223	
224	Streamed at a flat 20Hz while GRIPPED. Never authoritative — dropping every one of these packets must not change a throw's outcome, only degrade preview smoothness.
225	
226	```json
227	{ "type":"AIM", "roomCode":"ABCD", "playerId":"AJ", "seq":142,
228	  "aimDeg":-8.5, "attackAngleDeg":22.0, "rollDeg":4.0, "windup":0.35 }
229	```
230	
231	`seq` is a monotonic counter. Unity discards any packet whose `seq` is not greater than the last one seen, which cheaply handles out-of-order and stale arrivals. `windup` is normalized current acceleration magnitude, driving a "charging" indicator.
232	
233	Flat 20Hz is ~1.5 KB/s for the single active player — trivial. Don't bother with deadbanding unless profiling says otherwise.
234	
235	### `THROW` — single, authoritative
236	
237	Computed once on release from the sample buffer:
238	
239	- **power** — peak magnitude of linear acceleration during the swing, clamped, mapped 0..1. Use peak, not integral: more forgiving and better matched to perceived effort.
240	- **timingQuality** — locate the acceleration peak; score from `|t_release − t_peak|`. This reproduces Skip Skimmer's "release at the right moment."
241	- **aimDeg** — `dYaw` at release: the pointing-vector bearing, integrated from the gyro
242	  rather than sampled from fused orientation (see "Yaw must not come from alpha"), over
243	  the **full rotation** rather than the ±45° this originally specified. The narrow clamp
244	  flattened every fast swing to the limit, so hard throws all reported the same aim. Zero
245	  means "along `AimPreview.ThrowForward`", which is derived from the aiming camera rather
246	  than being world +Z, so straight means straight to the player looking at the TV.
247	- **attackAngleDeg** — `dBeta` at release. The stone's pitch relative to the water; the single most important variable.
248	- **rollDeg** — `dGamma` at release
249	- **spinRate** — `rotationRate` magnitude at release, feeding gyroscopic stability
250	
251	```json
252	{ "type":"THROW", "roomCode":"ABCD", "playerId":"AJ",
253	  "power":0.72, "timingQuality":0.91, "aimDeg":-8.5,
254	  "attackAngleDeg":22.0, "rollDeg":4.0, "spinRate":190.0 }
255	```
256	
257	The split matters for robustness: network hiccups make the preview stutter but can never cause a "the game read my throw wrong" moment.
258	
259	---
260	
261	## TV aim preview (`Assets/Scripts/Game/AimPreview.cs`)
262	
263	**Required feature — the TV must give live aiming feedback.** At 20Hz over a jittery connection, naive application of incoming values will look choppy, so smoothing is not optional polish here; it's what makes the feature work at all.
264	
265	```
266	On AIM received:
267	  if (msg.seq <= lastSeq) return;        // stale or out-of-order
268	  lastSeq = msg.seq;
269	  targetAim = msg.aimDeg; targetAttack = msg.attackAngleDeg; ...
270	  lastAimTime = Time.time;
271	
272	Every frame:
273	  curAim    = Mathf.SmoothDampAngle(curAim,    targetAim,    ref vAim,    0.08f);
274	  curAttack = Mathf.SmoothDampAngle(curAttack, targetAttack, ref vAttack, 0.08f);
275	  if (Time.time - lastAimTime > 0.5f) FadeOutPreview();   // surfaces connection loss
276	```
277	
278	**What to render**, in priority order:

But there's a real vulnerability: if a player joins as one ID then sends another JOIN_ROOM with a different playerId, both entries point to the same socket in the players map. On close, only the current playerId gets removed, leaving the old one orphaned forever — that's a leaked player slot, the host never sees PLAYER_LEFT for the abandoned ID, and broadcasts keep trying to send to a dead socket. A single connection could also fill the room to capacity by repeatedly joining with different IDs. Same issue happens when switching rooms: the old room's player entry never gets cleaned up, so that slot stays blocked even after the socket leaves.

The host also has a blind spot: when closeRoom runs, it only iterates through players and never notifies the host socket itself. More critically, this creates head-of-line blocking on the AIM stream: if the Unity host or phone's downlink stalls even briefly, queued frames pile up in the kernel buffer and arrive late, making the aim visibly lag behind. Scenes don't have a serialized relay URL stored anywhere, so I'll go with the default of ws://localhost:3000 for the local connection. The relay adds minimal latency on the host side, but the real network overhead comes from the phone communicating through cloudflared.

Now I have what I need to write the report. I'm identifying the critical code paths: the message handler and rate limiting around line 340, JSON parsing at 345, relay dispatch at 369-370, and the relayToHost and relayToPlayers functions that handle forwarding. I'm also noting the send function and constants that matter.

There's a slot leak bug where rejoining under a different player ID or switching rooms leaves stale map entries because handleJoinRoom never cleans up the socket's old registration—a player could join as one name, reconnect with a different one, and the old entry stays pinned forever, blocking slots and preventing the host from seeing a proper PLAYER_LEFT message. The controller might not actually rejoin with different IDs since credentials are set once, but the vulnerability is there for any client, and room-switching is trivially reachable.

The more serious issue is that closeRoom never notifies the host socket or resets it, so after an idle timeout the host stays stuck with a dead room code, can't CREATE_ROOM again because it's already registered, and has no recovery path since Unity only sends CREATE_ROOM on initial connect. After four hours of inactivity the host is permanently bricked.

There's also a backpressure issue I'm starting to examine.

I've confirmed the seq bug is already patched, so I have what I need for a comprehensive report. Now I'm compiling the final version with exact line numbers and code excerpts. I should also verify the hot path claim by checking how `send()` handles all message types including broadcasts, and how `relayToPlayers` re-serializes data for each recipient. There's also an important detail about `relayToHost` mutating the parsed object before stringifying it again.

The parse-mutate-stringify cycle happens roughly 60 times per second per AIM frame, but the actual cost is just microseconds—nowhere near the source of the lag we're seeing. The total relay-added latency is sub-millisecond on loopback, so I should make that clear in the report. Time to write it up.
